text: .2181 Prostatitis, p.2181 Renal calculi, p.2181 Renal colic, p.2182 Renal failure, p.2182 Sexually transmitted diseases, p.2182 Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, p.2182 Urinary-tract infections, p.2182 This chapter includes a number of drugs used in the management of certain urological or urogenital condi- tions such as urinary incontinence, benign prostatic hy- perplasia, and erectile dysfunction. Other drugs used in these conditions may be found elsewhere in Martindale: they include the tricyclic antidepressants such as imipramine (p.400) and the se- rotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor duloxet- ine (p.389), which are in the chapter on Antidepres- sants (p.372); some alpha blockers such as doxazosin (p.1275), phentolamine (p.1370), and prazosin (p.1375), as well as, more generally, diuretics and drugs such as ACE inhibitors which may be used to alter urological function, all of which are to be found in the chapter on Cardiovascular Drugs (p.1152); and the various electrolytes (see p.1667). For the treatment of urogenital infections, see under Choice of Antibacterial, p.162. For the management of urological and reproductive tract malignancies, see un- der Choice of Antineoplastic, p.643. Benign prostatic hyperplasia Benign enlargement of the prostate gland is common in men with increasing age: at least 50% of men aged over 60 years have histological evidence of hyperplasia. Men with an enlarged prostate may exhibit symptoms of lower uri- nary tract obstruction, such as acute or chronic urinary re- tention, or irritative symptoms such as frequency, urgency, nocturia, or occasionally urge incontinence, resulting from secondary bladder instability. Therapy is influenced by the severity of symptoms and their effect on the patient’s qual- ity of life. The three main options for management are watchful waiting (monitoring without active intervention), drug treatment, and surgery.1-7 Watchful waiting is suitable for men with mild to moder- ate symptoms that are not bothersome,3 and for some men with moderate to severe symptoms who have not yet de- veloped complications of benign prostatic hyperplasia such as renal impairment, urinary retention, or recurrent infection.2 The patient is monitored and advised on life- style measures that may improve symptoms; these include decreasing fluid intake at specific times such as bedtime or when going out, reducing caffeine and alcohol intake in general, and bladder re-training techniques. Drug treatment is essentially based on the use of alpha1- adrenoceptor blockers and 5α-reductase inhibitors, and is begun once symptoms become bothersome. • Alpha1-adre
